Deemed University Status for Kerala Kalamandalam 
*462.    SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
SHRI V. V. RAGHAVAN:† 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the request for treating Kerala Kalamandalam, Cheruthiruthy, 
Kerala, as a Deemed University is pending for a long time; 
(b) whether this institution has fulfilled all the formalities for the purpose; 
and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons for delaying the decision on 
the request? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) to (c) The proposal 
Kerala Kalamandalam for granting Deemed to be University status was received 
and referred to UGC for examination and their recommendation/comments. 
Declaration of an institution as Deemed University is a statutory process done 
on fulfilment of several requirements under the guidelines. UGC has inforlned 
that the proposal has been examined and it has been decided to send an Expert 
Committee to make an on the spot exam iniation of the proposal. The Expert 
Committee has been constituted and is likely to visit the Institution shortly to 
examine in detail the in frastructural facilities, academic and research 
programmes offered by the Institute etc. 
SHRI V. V. RAGHAVAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the proposal for treating 
the Kerala Kalamandalam as a Deemed University is pending with the U.G.C. 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri V. V Raghavan.

Platform at Birur Junction 
*463. SHRI K. C. KONDAIAH: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the platform at Birur junction railway station 
has not been raised to suit broad gauge trains; 
(b) if so, whether the old people, women and children have to steeply 
climb down from the train at Platform No. 2 and again to get the Birur-Shimoga 
passenger train and vice-versa; and 
(c) if so, whether Government would take steps in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to (c) 
A statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. All the platforms at Birur are suitable for broad gauge trains. 
(b) and (c) Platform No. 1 has been raised to high level in February, 
2000. As regards raising of platform nos. 2 and 3, the work has been sanctioned 
and will be taken up shortly. 
SHRI K. C. KONDAIAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the Railways took up the 
gauge conversion during 1991—96 in Karnataka; and completed it very fast. 
But, unfortunately, the Railways did not think of providing platforms and

Crop loan insurance scheme 
*464. SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state:  
(a) the amount released so far to States for implementation of crop loan 
insurance scheme, State- wise; 
(b) in which States such facilities are available now; and 
           (c) the measures taken by Government for continuation of crop loans to 
the needy farmers of North-Eastern States? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) No State-wise releases are made  by the Government of India (Gol) 
under National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS). However, as per 
provision of the scheme, Gol makes available its share (50%) of financial 
liabilities on account of making payment of insurance claims; premia-subsidy; 
administrative and operational expenses etc. to General Insurance Corporation 
of India (GIC) which is the Implementing Agency (IA) of the scheme. 
The amount released to GIC so fa r by the Gol for the implementation 
of NAIS is given as under:- 
Year Amount Releasd 
(Rs. in crores) 
1999-2000 46.68 
2000-2001 139.00 
2001-2002 195.00 (Till date) 
(b) NAIS is voluntary in nature and available for implementation to all 
the States/Union Territories. So far, following States/Union Territories have 
opted for the implementation of the scheme:- 
1 .Andhra Pradesh, 2. Assam, 3. Bihar, 4. Chhattisgarh, 5. Goa, 6. Gujarat, 
7. Himachal Pradesh, 8. Jharkhand, 9.  Karnataka, 10. Kerala, 11. Madhya 
Pradesh, 12. Maharashtra, 13. Meghalay a, 14. Orissa, 15. Sikkim, 16. Tamil 
Nadu, 17. Uttar Pradesh, 18. West Bengal, 19. Andaman & Nicobar Islands, 
20. Pondicherry.

Illegal import of genetically engineered foods 
*461. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will th e Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the situation arising out of entering 
of Genetically Engineered (GE) foods illegally into the country, if so, what 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2001 ] 
steps have been taken to stop these to flood the markets; and 
(b) the number of such products confiscated and the persons involved, 
arrested? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) 
The Government of India have not ye t accorded approval for import, export 
commercial production, storage, handling and marketing of any Genetically 
Engineered Food in the country. As per the Environment (Protection) Act, 
1986 and Rules 1989, it is mandatory that all such products obtain the approval 
of Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) of the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests from bio-safety (environmental and food safety) angle 
for use and sale in the country. 
Further, action has been taken by the Ministry of Environment and Forests 
to enlarge the scope of Ru le 11 of Environment (Protection) Rules 1989 for 
obtaining a mandatory declaration as to whether the commodity being imported 
is Genetically Modified/Engineered or not. 
Any violation of the Environment (Protection) Act and Rules is 
prosecutable. So far, no such consignment has been confiscated nor any one 
prosecuted or arrested.

Contract Farming, however, is already being practiced in different States for 
production of various crops such as sugarcane, tobacco, oil palm, horticultural 
crops, plantation crops, etc. besides production of seeds of different crops. 
Under the contract farming arrangements, the farmers carry on cultiva-
tion on contract basis with buy-back arrangements with the companies including 
multinational companies. Contract farming promotes and facilitate transfer of

Cut in Railway expenditure 
*478. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the operating ratio of the Railways has been 
worsening over the years, rising to 98.8 per cent, as per the estimates of 2000-
2001; 
(b) if so, whether the Railways are considering to launch an all-out drive 
to cut its expenditure, without cutting the current plan size, in any way; 
(c) what are the Major Heads under which expenditure is proposed to be 
cut and what is the targeted percentage of cut; and 
(d) what was the actual operating cost in 2000-2001 viz-a-viz the estimates 
for that year? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to (c) 
Yes Sir. The operating ratio of the Railways has been deteriorating since 
1995-96 mainly due to implementation of the recommendations of the Vth 
Central Pay Commjssion which increased the working expenses inordinately 
due to steep rise in the staff cost s on Railways. The Ordinary Working 
Expenses rose from Rs. 16186 crore in 1996-97 to Rs. 27534 crore in 2000-01 
(Provl.) registering a growth of 70%. The pension expenditure also increased 
from Rs. 2509 crore to around Rs. 5100 crore during this period, an increase of 
almost 100%. The earnings, however, could not keep pace with the growth in 
expenditure mainly due to sharp reduction in loading in 1998-99 as a result of 
economic slow-down. The co mbined effect of increase in staff expenditure 
and the earnings not keeping pace has resulted in deterioration of the 
Operating Ratio. In 2000-01, the operating ratio was originally budgeted at 
98.8% but it has marginally improved to 98.3% (Provisional) in the actuals. 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2001 ] 
The Railways have been making vigorous efforts to improve the operating 
ratio by controlling expenditure and augmenting earnings. Some of the 
important measures being teken include: 
(i) Measures to control expenditure by improving staff productivity, 
assets utilisation, inventory management, fuel consumption, austerity 
in areas such as travel, publicity, hospitality etc. 
(ii) For improving earnings, aggressive marketing with improve freight 
services and commercial incentives. 
(iii) All efforts are being made to curb leakage of revenue and pilferages. 
The Zonal Railways have also been asked to effect savings in Ordinary 
Working Expenses, which are spread over Demands for Grants 3 to 12 of the 
Railways, by around 900 crore in 2001-02. This works to around 3% of the 
total Ordinary Working Expenses. As of now there is no cut in the plan size of 
the Railways. 
(d) In the year 2000-01, the actuals of the Ordinary Working Expenses, 
which represent mainly the maintenance and the operating costs of the 
Railways, are Rs 27,534 crore (Provisional) as against Rs. 27,815 crore in the 
Revised Estimates.

Market access for farm exports 
3538. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian agriculture has become increasingly 
non-competitive in the wo rld market because of h eavy subsidization by the 
developed countries; and 
(b) if so, what steps Government have taken or propose to take to ensure 
greater market access for its farm exports abroad? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) The 
competitiveness of commodities depend on various factors including cost of 
production, quality, consumers' preferences , etc. It may, thus, not be correct 
to attribute in general the uncompetitiveness of all agricultural products only 
to the heavy subsidization in the developed countries. However, keeping in 
view the trade disortive nature of subsidies provided in the developed countries, 
India, in its negotiating proposal submitted to the World Trade Organisation 
(WTO), has sought enhanced market access for its farm products by demanding 
a substantial reduction in tariffs and elimination of export subsidies and 
substantial reduction in domestic support by the developed countries. 
(b) Policy of exports of agricultural products forms an integral part of 
the Export / Import Policy of the country. The policy regarding the exports of 
agricultural products is governed principally by the concerns of India's food 
security, maximising farm incomes and earning foreign exchange. Review of 
export performance of agricultural products is an ongoing process, and 
accordingly, policy interventions are made as and when considered necessary 
with a view to making agricultural exports increasingly viable. The long-term 
Export Policy lays stress on the promotion of agricultural exports. The Policy 
envisages the creation of Agri. Export Zones for the end to end development 
for export of specific products from a geographically contiguous area. These 
zones are to be identified by the respective State Governments who would 
also evolve a comprehensive package of services such as provision of pre-/ 
post-harvest treatment and operations, plant protection, processing, storage 
and related research and development. The agro sector can also avail of the 
60 

[24 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Exim Policy Schemes like Duty Exemption Scheme and Export Capital Goods 
Scheme. The recent Exim Policy announc ed by the Government on the 31st 
March, 2001, also envisages the entitlement of Agri exporters for recognition 
as Export House / Trading House / Star Trading House / Super Star Trading 
House on achieving l/3rd of the threshold limit prescribed for exports of other 
goods.

Changes in the price of medicines, like other commodities, is a normal feature. 
For a scheduled formulation, a manufacturer is required to follow the price 
fixed by the Government. If the Government notifies ceiling price in case of 
any scheduled formulation, it has to be followed by all manufacturers. Prices 
of non-scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers themselves. 
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) nevertheless monitors 
the movement of prices of non-scheduled formulations and intervenes whenever 
necessary in the public interest. 
An analysis of the prices of 206 medicines representing different 
therapeutic groups published in ORG- MARG for the period December, 1999 
- December, 2000, shows that while the prices of 18 formulations came down, 
those of 86 remained unchanged. The prices of 102 formulations showed an 
upward trend. Of these, 43 went up by less than 5% 31 between 5 and 10%, 20 
between 10 and 20% and the remaining 8 formulations by between 20 to 50%. 
Major factors which normally contribute to increase in prices of medicines 
are cost of raw materials, (active ingredients, excipients and packing materials 
etc.,), processing and packaging costs, cost of sales promotion, R&D cost, 
etc;.

Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority has filed two additional affidavits explaining 
its mechanism of monitoring and regulating the prices of scheduled and non-

Smuggling of rare birds 
3556. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister 
of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 1200 rare birds were seized recently at Indira 
Gandhi Airport, New Delhi; 
(b) if so, the kinds of the birds so seized; 
(c) whether smuggling of such birds has been going on during the last 
three years; if so, State-wise details thereof; and 
(d) the steps being taken by Government to protect birds from smuggling? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. On 13.5.2001, 1200 Red Munia and 33 
Alexandrine parakeets were seized by Cu stoms with the help of Officials of 
Ministry of Environment and Forests at Indira Gandhi Airport, which were 
being smuggled to Sharjah. 
(c) Reports of smuggling of birds have come to the notice of this Ministry 
from time to time. The details of seizure of birds, during the last three years, 
as reported by the Regional Dy. Direct ors, Wildlife Preservation, located at 
Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai is given in the Statement, {See below). 
State-wise details of smuggling of birds are not compiled and collected at the 
level of the Central Government. 
(d) Steps taken by the Government to protect birds from smuggling are 
as follows: 
(1) Steps taken at the State level: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting 
and commercial exploitation under the provisions of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
77 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2001 ] 
(ii) State level and District level coordination Committees have been 
set up in several States to prevent poaching and illegal trade in 
wildlife. 
(iii) State Wildlife Authorities carry out regular checking of the stocks 
of dealers in birds. 
(2) Steps taken at National level 
(i) Government of India has set up regional and Sub-regional Offices 
for wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the 
country to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(ii) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under 
the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute 
wildlife offenders. Anti-poaching efforts are being coordinated with 
INTERPOL. 
(iii) Financial and technical help is being extended to the States under 
various Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project 
Elephant, Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-
development around Protected Areas for enhancing the capacity and 
infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to wild 
animals . Financial assistance is, in particular, being provided for 
raising 'Strike Forces' and providing arms to the protection staff for 
combating the organised poachers. Assistance is also provided for 
giving rewards to the., informers for eliciting information about 
poachers and smugglers. 
(iv) A Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set 
up under the chairmanship of Se cretary, Environment & Forests, 
Government of India, for control of poaching and illegal trade in 
wildlife. 
(v) Export of wild animals and their derivatives is prohibited under 
EXIM policy. 
(vi) A National Conference of Forests and Environment Ministers of 
State Government was held on 29th and 30th January, 2001. It was 
resolved to organise existing protection staff into viable formations 
for effective control of poach ing and to create inforcement 
infrastructure both within and outside protected areas. 
78 

[24 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(vii) Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments 
to lend a helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching and 
illegal trade in wildlife. 
(3) Steps taken at International level 
(i) Government of India seeks international co-operation under the 
provisions of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered 
Species of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) for control of illegal trade 
in wildlife items. 
(ii) To control transboundary trade a protocol has been signed with 
Peoples' Republic of China and a MoU has been signed with His 
Majesty's Government of Nepal. 
(iii) A Global Tiger Forum of Tiger Range Countries has been created 
for addressing international issues related to Tiger Conservation.

and to prevent poaching? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Lion is found only in Gir Ecosystem in Gujarat. Recent

(c) The steps taken by the Government to protect and prevent poaching 
of wild cats are as follows: 
(1) Steps taken at the State level: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting 
and commercial exploitation under the provisions of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) State level and District level coordination committees have been set 
up in several States to prevent poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(2) Steps taken at National level: 
(i) Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-Regional Offices 
for wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the 
country to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
97 

 RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2001] 
(ii)  Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute wildlife 
offenders. Anti poaching efforts are being coordinated with INTERPOL. 
(iii)   Financial and technical help is being extended to the States under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project Elephant, 
Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-Development 
around Protected Areas for enhancing the capacity and infrastructure of 
the States for providing effective protection to wild animals. Financial 
assistance is in particular, being provided for raising 'Strike Forces' and 
providing arms to the protection staff for combating the organised 
poachers. Assistance is also provided for giving rewards to the informers 
for eliciting information about poachers and smugglers. 
(iv)  A Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set up under 
the chairmanship of Secretary, Environment & Forests, Government of 
India, for control of poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(v)  Export of wild animals and their derivatives is prohibited under EXIM 
policy.        t 
(vi)  A National Conference of Forests and Environment Ministers of State 
Government was held on 29th and 30th January, 2001. It was resolved to 
organise existing protection staff into viable formations for effective 
control of poaching and to create enforcement infrastructure both 
within and out side protected areas. 
(vii)    Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments to lend 
a helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching and illegal trade 
in wildlife. 
(3) Steps taken at International level 
(i) Government of India seeks international co-operation under the 
provisions of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species 
of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) for control of illegal trade in wildlife 
items. 
(ii) To control transboundary trade a protocol has been signed with Peoples' 
Republic of China and a MoU has b een signed with His Majesty's 
Government of Nepal. 
98

for addressing international issues related to Tiger Conservation.

Schemes/Programmes for Promotion, Expansion and Propagation of Hindi 
and Sanskrit 
HINDI: 
(i) Appointment of Hindi Teachers: This Ministry implements the 
scheme of financial assistance for the appointment and training of 
Hindi teachers in non-Hindi speaking States/UTs. Under the scheme, 
100% Central assistance is provided to States/UTs for the 
appointment and training of Hindi teachers and to establish training 
colleges for trained Hindi teachers. 
(ii) Central Hindi Directorate: Implements (i) scheme of teaching Hindi 
as a second language to the peop le of non-Hindi speaking States 
through corresp ondence (ii) scheme of financial assistance for 
promotion and development of Hindi to NGOs specially located in 
non-Hindi speaking States (iii) scheme of preparation of Bilingual, 
Trilingual and Multilingual dictionaries and Conversational guides, 
(iv) scheme of organizing workshops and study tours for non-Hindi 
writers of Non-Hindi speaking States, (v) scheme of free distribution 
of Hindi books to institutions, Central Schools and libraries located 
in non-Hindi speaking States, (vi) scheme of awards to Hindi writers 
of non-Hindi speaking States.(vii) Exhibition of published books of 
CHD. 
(iii) Commission for Scientific and Technical Terminology: has been 
engaged in the task of evolving technical terms in Hindi, producing 
University Level Text Books, definitional Dictionaries and various 
reference literature. 
(iv) Kendriya Hindi Shikshan Mandal, Agra: runs the Kendriya Hindi 
Sansthan with its Head Quarters at Agra and its Centres at Delhi, 
Hyderabad, Mysore, Guwahati and Shillong. The Sansthan conducts 
Hindi Shikshan Nishat (M.Ed level) Hindi Shikshan Parangat (B. 
Ed. level), Hindi Shikshan Prav een, a four-year Hindi Shikshan 
Diploma and other intensive Hind i teaching orientation courses. 
The Sansthan also runs courses for the teaching of Hindi to foreigners 
at Agra under the Scheme of "Propagation of Hindi Abroad". It 
publishes research-oriented material related to Hindi language and

Literature. Under the scheme, Hindi Sevi Samman Yojana, thirteen 
Eminent Hindi Scholars are sel ected every year  for. their 
distinguished contribution to Hindi, research and creative literature. 
SANSKRIT: 
(i) Development of Sanskrit Education : Under the Central Plan Scheme 
of Development of Sanskrit Education, financial assistance is granted 
to Eminent Sanskrit Pandits in indigent circumstances, scholarships 
given to students of High/Higher Secondary Schools, assistance 
provided for the teaching of Sanskrit in Secondary Schools, for the 
Modernization of Sanskrit Pathshalas and other grants given to State 
Governments for various schemes for the promotion of Sanskrit. 
Under the Central Scheme, financial assistance to Deemed 
Universities/CBSE/NCERT/SCERT etc. is also given to improve 
the methodology of teaching Sanskrit in schools. 
(ii) Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan: (an autonomous organisation of the 
Government) implements various schemes and programmes through 
its 8 constituent Vidypeethas/Shodh Sansthans and 21 Adarsh 
Mahvidyalayas. These includes teaching courses, research 
programmes, publications, correspondence courses and the 
development of traditional curriculums. 
(iii) Mahrshi Sandipani Rashtriya Ved Vidya Pratishthan, Ujjain, (an 
autonomous organization under the Ministry of HRD) undertakes 
various activities including support to traditional vedic institutions 
and scholars and providing scholarships/fellowships for the 
promotion of vedic studies and research.

Vidyapeetha, New Delhi and Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha, 
Tirupati impart education at various levels through the medium of 
Sanskrit and offer facilities for research. In addition, 435 Sanskrit 
centres in various Universities and colleges are being run by the 
University Grants Commission.

 one that we have.   Sir, because of this reluctance, based upon a fanciful
